books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: Henry Highland Garnet, “An Address to the Slaves of the United States,” 1843

stimulus.text:
"Brethren, arise, arise! Strike for your lives and liberties. Now is the day and the hour. . . . Rather die freemen than live to be slaves. Remember that you are FOUR MILLIONS!" — Henry Highland Garnet, "An Address to the Slaves of the United States," National Negro Convention, Buffalo, New York, August 1843.

"Right is of no Sex—Truth is of no Color—God is the Father of us all, and we are all brethren." — Motto of The North Star, Frederick Douglass’s newspaper, first issue, December 3, 1847.

The convention refused to endorse Garnet’s address, by a single vote, and Douglass spoke against it.
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotations: Henry Highland Garnet, “An Address to the Slaves of the United States,” National Negro Convention, Buffalo, August 1843; motto of The North Star, first issue, December 3, 1847. Wording checked against BlackPast and the Library of Congress.

source: original; stimuli are verbatim public-domain quotations from Garnet (1843) and The North Star (1847)
stem: Garnet’s call differs from Garrison’s moral suasion mainly in that Garnet

options.text: asked slaveholders to free their slaves gradually
options.misconception: Garnet demands rising now, not gradual freeing.

options.text: refused to speak to enslaved people directly
options.misconception: The address speaks directly to the slaves.

options.text: believed the Constitution protected slavery and must be condemned
options.misconception: That is Garrison’s view; Garnet disagreed with Garrison on the Constitution.

options.text: urged enslaved people themselves to rise and resist

rationales.A: Garnet does not ask for gradual freeing. He says: arise, strike for your lives and liberties, now is the day.
rationales.B: Garnet speaks straight to the slaves: brethren, arise. He does not speak past them.
rationales.C: Condemning the Constitution as proslavery was Garrison’s position. Garnet disagreed with Garrison on that point.
rationales.D: Garrison appealed to white consciences. Garnet called on enslaved people themselves to rise and resist.
rationales.general:
1. Hear Garnet’s words. Arise, arise, and strike for your lives and liberties.
2. Compare with moral suasion. Garrison appealed to the conscience of white Americans; Garnet appealed to enslaved people to act.
3. Name the difference. Who acts, and how.
Background: Garnet gave the address at the National Negro Convention in Buffalo in August 1843.
Remember: when two reformers differ, ask who each one asks to act.
